**The Doorframe**

The realtor said the marks would have to be painted over. Buyers didn't want other people's children on the walls, she said, and then she laughed a little, because she heard how it sounded. I told her I'd take care of it.

The house had been empty since March. I hadn't been back since the funeral, and even then I'd only stood in the kitchen for twenty minutes while my sister handled the casseroles. Now it was July and the air inside had that held-breath quality of a place no one has moved through in a while. Dust on the banister. A calendar in the kitchen still turned to February, a dentist's appointment circled in blue that my mother had not lived to keep.

The marks were on the frame between the kitchen and the hallway. I'd forgotten about them, which seems impossible now. Every birthday from three to seventeen, my mother stood me against that frame with a hardcover book flat on my head and drew a line in pencil, then wrote my initials and the year. I remember the book was always the same one, a green atlas, because it was the heaviest thing on the shelf and she said a heavy book kept a boy honest. I remember the cold of the frame against my heels. I remember the year I was fourteen and had grown almost four inches and she said *well* and nothing else, and I understood that I had crossed some line that wasn't drawn in pencil.

I stood there for a while with the paint can at my feet and read them like a column in a ledger. 1988, 1989, 1990. The handwriting stayed the same while I climbed past it. By 1999 the top mark was a little above my mother's own head, and there I stopped, because that was the year I left, and she didn't measure me when I came home at Christmas. I was a grown man. You don't measure a grown man.

Except there were marks above that.

I had to squint. The pencil was lighter, fainter, as if pressed by a hand that didn't want to commit. There were no initials. Just dates. 2006. 2011. 2015. 2019. 2022. Each one a little below the one before it.

It took me longer than it should have to understand. I think I actually looked around the room, as if a nephew I'd forgotten about might be standing there, waiting to be explained. And then I looked at the spacing again—a quarter inch, half an inch, most of an inch in the last gap—and I put my hand on the frame at the 2022 line and it came to just about my collarbone, and I knew.

She'd been measuring herself.

I don't know how she did it alone. You can't put a book on your own head and mark the wall with any accuracy; the geometry is against you. Maybe she used a level. Maybe she stood there in the kitchen with a yardstick and a mirror, an eighty-year-old woman working out an engineering problem so that she could write down, in her own house, in her own hand, that she was getting smaller. Maybe a neighbor helped. I like that less. I want it to have been just her.

The realtor's word for it, if I'd told her, would have been *sad*. And it is that, I suppose. But standing there I felt something closer to the opposite, a kind of fierce, unexpected pride, the way you feel when someone you love does something difficult without asking anyone's permission. She had spent fifteen years drawing a line under a boy who kept getting taller. Then the boy left and the drawing stopped, and I imagine the doorframe just sat there for a while being a doorframe. And then one day, for reasons she never mentioned to me or to my sister or to anyone, she decided the record wasn't finished. That the house should know what was happening to the person in it. That shrinking was as much a fact as growing, and facts get written down.

My mother was not a sentimental woman. She didn't keep my drawings or my report cards. She threw out the atlas when the spine went. But she kept a pencil in the drawer nearest that doorframe until the day she died—I checked; it's still there, a yellow Ticonderoga sharpened to nearly nothing—and every few years she took it out and told the truth about herself to a piece of wood.

I didn't paint the frame.

I called the realtor and told her the house would be listed as is, and if a buyer wanted the marks gone they could do it themselves after closing. She said that was unusual. I said I knew. She said, in the voice of someone who has decided to stop arguing, that some people actually liked that kind of thing, that it gave a house *character*, and I let her believe that was what I was thinking.

Before I left I took the pencil from the drawer. I stood in the doorway with my back against the frame, heels cold against the wood the way they had been forty years ago, and I reached up and made a mark above my head, as level as I could manage without the atlas. It's crooked. I wrote the year beside it. I didn't write my initials, because she hadn't written hers, and it seemed important to follow the form.

I'm not sure what the next owner will make of it. A column of a child's growth, a gap of seven years, then a slow descent, then one uncertain line near the top with a fresh date and no name. Maybe they'll think it's a mistake. Maybe they'll paint it. But it's possible, I think, that someone will stand there the way I did and work out the geometry of it, and understand that a house can hold more than one kind of measurement, and that both of them count.
